Q: b64encode() / b64decode - unbalanced encoding A:

The simple answer is skip all the intermediate (and inconsistent) encode/decode. The input string should be bytes:

import base64

in_str = bytes(range(33,127))
intermediate_str = base64.b64encode(in_str)
out_str = base64.b64decode(intermediate_str)

print(f"{in_str = }")
print(f"{intermediate_str = }")
print(f"{out_str = }")
print(in_str == out_str)

Output:

in_str = b'!"#$%&\'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[\\]^_`abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{|}~'
intermediate_str = b'ISIjJCUmJygpKissLS4vMDEyMzQ1Njc4OTo7PD0+P0BBQkNERUZHSElKS0xNTk9QUVJTVFVWV1hZWltcXV5fYGFiY2RlZmdoaWprbG1ub3BxcnN0dXZ3eHl6e3x9fg=='
out_str = b'!"#$%&\'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[\\]^_`abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{|}~'
True

If you input string is more complicated than ASCII, use the default encode/decode which uses UTF-8:

import base64

in_str = '我的名字是马克。'
intermediate_str = base64.b64encode(in_str.encode())
out_str = base64.b64decode(intermediate_str).decode()

print(f"{in_str = }")
print(f"{intermediate_str = }")
print(f"{out_str = }")
print(in_str == out_str)

Output:

in_str = '我的名字是马克。'
intermediate_str = b'5oiR55qE5ZCN5a2X5piv6ams5YWL44CC'
out_str = '我的名字是马克。'
True

You can use any encoding that works with the Unicode codepoints involved, just be consistent. In the case below 'chinese' results in fewer encoded bytes than UTF-8.

import base64

in_str = '我的名字是马克。'
intermediate_str = base64.b64encode(in_str.encode('chinese'))
out_str = base64.b64decode(intermediate_str).decode('chinese')

print(f"{in_str = }")
print(f"{intermediate_str = }")
print(f"{out_str = }")
print(in_str == out_str)

Output:

in_str = '我的名字是马克。'
intermediate_str = b'ztK1xMP719bKx8Ltv8uhow=='
out_str = '我的名字是马克。'
True

Q: Is replaying a transactional outbox in auto-increment ID order will maintain the order of events? A:

This can never work.

Imagine two concurrent transactions modifying two rows in the same table:

Transaction 1                         Transaction 2
=============                         =============

start transaction (event 101)
                                      start transaction (event 102)

update row 1

                                      update row 1

                                      update row 2

update row 2

write outbox
                                      write outbox
commit
                                      commit

Transaction 1 modifies row 1 before transaction 2 does, but transaction 2 modifies row 2 before transaction 1. No matter how you serialize these two transactions, the result would never be the same as the original.

The only way you could get this to work is to serialize the original transactions, so that no two of them can run concurrently. That is safe, but horrible for concurrency, particularly if these transactions are not very short.

One way to serialize transactions is to use advisory locks:

START TRANSACTION;

/*
 * Take a transaction-level advisory lock.
 * "4711" is an arbitrary number; you have to use the same
 * number in all transactions to use the same lock.
 */
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(4711);

/* get the event number */
SELECT nextval('event_sequence');

/* perform all your activities */
UPDATE ...;

INSERT INTO outbox VALUES (...);

COMMIT;

A potential alternative to strict serialization is to use the SERIALIZABLE isolation level for all your transactions. That will make sure that the transactions can be serialized (even if they run concurrently). But then you never know which transaction is logically earlier, so you don't know how to assign event numbers.

Q: Power Pivot table returns only grand total for every row label, despite relationship existing A:

I don't see need to split table and create a relationship. Just aggregate on exploded rows.

Following is M code generated (with guidance from CoPilot) and tested:

let
    Source = Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Table1"]}[Content],
    #"Split Column by Delimiter" = Table.ExpandListColumn(Table.TransformColumns(Source, 
          {{"AnimalType", Splitter.SplitTextByDelimiter(",", QuoteStyle.Csv), 
          let itemType = (type nullable text) meta [Serialized.Text = true] in type {itemType}}}), "AnimalType"),
    #"ChangedType" = Table.TransformColumnTypes(#"Split Column by Delimiter",{{"AnimalType", type text}}),
    #"TrimmedText" = Table.TransformColumns(#"ChangedType",{{"AnimalType", Text.Trim, type text}}),
    #"FilteredRows" = Table.SelectRows(#"TrimmedText", each ([AnimalType] <> null)),
    #"GroupedRows" = Table.Group(#"FilteredRows", {"AnimalType"}, {{"CountType", each Table.RowCount(_), Int64.Type}}),
    TotalValue = List.Sum(#"GroupedRows"[CountType]),
    TotalRow = #table({"AnimalType", "CountType"},{{"Grand Total", TotalValue}}),
    #"Final Table" = Table.Combine({#"GroupedRows", TotalRow})
in
    #"Final Table"

This is output from sample data provided:

AnimalType CountType
1 Mammals 2
2 Reptiles 1
3 Grand Total 3

Note that I removed spaces and symbols from header names of sample data.
